tools.name: search_assets
tools.title: Search assets
tools.description: Search the item library (furniture, fixtures, lights, plants, outdoor) by keyword, with one or several queries in a call. The catalog is a limited set that varies by server: what a search returns is what exists. Results provide valid asset ids and placement facts when these are not already known. A query matches the items whose name, id, category or tags hold every one of its words. Returns one group per query, each item with its id, name, category, dimensions [width, height, depth] in metres and attachTo (null on the floor, else 'wall', 'wall-side' or 'ceiling'). Related lookups (sofa, coffee table, tv stand) can share a call.

category.description: Only items of this category (furniture, kitchen, bathroom, outdoor, …).

queries.description: One or more searches to run in a single call.

tools.name: view_assets
tools.title: View catalog items
tools.description: Pictures of catalog items by id, each with its size and the names of its paintable surfaces (paint takes one as role).

ids.description: One to six catalog item ids, as search_assets or furnish_room returned them.

tools.name: search_materials
tools.title: Search materials
tools.description: Search or browse the material library (the finishes paint gives), several queries in one call: find a library material's ref here rather than guessing it. The library is Pascal's materials and, in the editor, the ones it holds besides (the community's, yours, your workspace's). A query's words match the words of a material's id, name and kind, or a piece of its id (plank48, cco), building words as the library writes them (timber is wood, weatherboard is siding, render is stucco), colour words by its shade (dark, light, white, grey) and surface words (roof, wall, floor, ceiling) by what it suits; a word of one or two letters, or one as common as 'the', searches nothing. Without a query, a browse lists by name every material of its kind, or that suits its surface (flat colours suit every one), or the whole library. Returns one group per query: each material's ref (library:<id>), name, kind, the surfaces it suits and its colour, best first (a browse by name), 12 at a time for a search and 150 for a browse; the words no material answers (missing), so a finish the library lacks is said, not guessed; and on a long list how many more there are (more) and the offset that lists them (next).

query.description: Search words, e.g. "white render", "grey metal roofing", "oak floor"; leave them out to browse.

surface.description: Only materials that suit this surface; flat colours suit every one.

offset.description: The next page of a long search or browse: the next it returned.

queries.description: One or more searches or browses to run in one call.

tools.name: cut_floor_opening
tools.title: Cut floor or ceiling opening
tools.description: Create a persistent opening on a room or level from a polygon or rectangle. A floor cut also opens the automatic ceiling directly below; a ceiling cut can also open the floor above. Use cutsAdjacent:false for a one-surface cut. A mezzanine room cuts only its own plate. levelIds repeats the opening as a shaft on several levels.

width.description: In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Must be greater than 0 m.

depth.description: In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Must be greater than 0 m.

tools.name: remove_floor_opening
tools.title: Remove floor opening
tools.description: Remove an authored floor or ceiling opening and restore the derived surfaces it cut.

tools.name: set_floor_foundation
tools.title: Set floor and foundation
tools.description: Supply slabId or slabIds; grouped plates receive the same floor-top displacement, while edge slots apply only to the first plate. A ground-contact floor has two inputs: thickness (slab, min 0.01 m, grows upward from the foundation) and foundationHeight (0 = on the ground, no foundation; > 0 = raised on a solid foundation; foundation.type "solid" alone raises it 0.3 m, "none" puts it on the ground). The floor top is derived and never floats: grade + foundationHeight + thickness; everything the floor carries (walls, openings, items, rooms, storeys above) moves with the top. Legacy floorHeight (a target top) maps to foundationHeight = top - grade - thickness, never below 0; null = on the ground. On upper plates the underside stays on the walls below: thickness (or floorHeight as a target top) changes the top; only ground-contact plates accept a foundation. Explicit room floors translate with the floor to preserve steps.

thickness.description: Slab thickness in meters. On the ground it sits on the foundation (or the ground) and grows upward: a thicker slab raises the floor top and everything on it. Never below 0.01 m (smaller values are clamped). Upstairs the underside stays on the walls below. In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Minimum 0 m.

foundationHeight.description: Ground-bearing floors only: height of the foundation under the slab, in meters. 0 = on the ground (no foundation); > 0 = raised on a solid foundation. The floor top is derived: grade + foundationHeight + thickness. In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Minimum 0 m.

anyOf.description: Legacy: a target floor top in level-local meters. On the ground it is mapped to foundationHeight = top - grade - thickness (never below 0); null = on the ground. Prefer thickness and foundationHeight. In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft").

tools.name: set_room_floor_construction
tools.title: Set room floor construction
tools.description: Edit the single floor volume associated with a room, with the same patch as set_floor_foundation. On a ground-contact floor: thickness (slab on the foundation, grows upward, min 0.01 m) and foundationHeight (0 = on the ground; > 0 = raised on a solid foundation); the top is derived as grade + foundationHeight + thickness and carries everything on the floor. A drawn slab takes thickness, finishes and a numeric floorHeight (its top) only. Supply slabId when the room spans multiple construction domains; an absorbed legacy slab is edited through its derived base plate.

thickness.description: Slab thickness in meters. On the ground it sits on the foundation (or the ground) and grows upward: a thicker slab raises the floor top and everything on it. Never below 0.01 m (smaller values are clamped). Upstairs the underside stays on the walls below. In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Minimum 0 m.

foundationHeight.description: Ground-bearing floors only: height of the foundation under the slab, in meters. 0 = on the ground (no foundation); > 0 = raised on a solid foundation. The floor top is derived: grade + foundationHeight + thickness. In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Minimum 0 m.

anyOf.description: Legacy: a target floor top in level-local meters. On the ground it is mapped to foundationHeight = top - grade - thickness (never below 0); null = on the ground. Prefer thickness and foundationHeight. In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft").

tools.name: rebase_floor_reference
tools.title: Rebase floor reference
tools.description: Change or clear one or more footprint reference datums in one atomic edit, compensating supported storey offsets so existing world geometry stays in place. Supply slabIds together for a shared storey.

anyOf.description: In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft").

tools.name: create_mezzanine
tools.title: Create mezzanine
tools.description: Add an open-below room inside a host reference polygon, with a separate thin plate and railings on open edges. Minimum area 1 m²; elevation defaults to half the storey snapped to 0.05 m, thickness to 0.2 m. Elevation must exceed thickness and stay at least 0.3 m below the resolved footprint plane; overlapping mezzanines are refused. The host floor and walls stay intact.

elevation.description: In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft").

thickness.description: In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Minimum 0.02 m.

tools.name: move_zone
tools.title: Move or rotate room
tools.description: Move room intent and contents. Shared walls and openings stay with neighbours; the room takes plain copies. Rotation is radians about Y, before translation, about the room centroid unless a pivot is supplied. Crossings split walls and overlaps re-derive rooms. Force can reposition obstructing openings when they fit; otherwise the edit is refused.

angle.description: In radians, or text with a unit ("90°").

tools.name: duplicate_zone
tools.title: Duplicate room
tools.description: Copy room intent and contents with fresh IDs; shared walls are copied without openings. Rotation is radians about Y before translation. Collinear destination walls are merged, preserving their IDs and hosted children. Crossings split walls and rooms re-derive; overlap is allowed. Force can reposition obstructing openings only when they fit.

angle.description: In radians, or text with a unit ("90°").

tools.name: rotate_zone
tools.title: Rotate room a quarter turn
tools.description: Rotate a room by quarterTurns 1 or -1 about its centroid, then align its first reference vertex to gridStep (default 0.5 m). Crossings split walls and collinear overlaps merge. Force can reposition obstructing openings only when they fit.

gridStep.description: In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Must be greater than 0 m.

tools.name: lock_outside_faces
tools.title: Keep outside dimensions
tools.description: Keep the building's outer size: put exterior wall faces on their fixed reference lines, moving wall bodies inward so walls thicken inward and later thickness edits preserve outer dimensions. Supply either levelId or zoneIds.

tools.name: set_zone_intent
tools.title: Set room intent
tools.description: Update room name, floor finish/elevation/regions, floor.footprint ("new" mints a unique floor key tied to this creator room, an existing key joins that floor on this level, null returns to the shared floor). Touching rooms with the same key share a base plate; disconnected pieces share construction settings. Conversion preserves world geometry in one edit and refuses when infeasible. get_zones exposes floor_choices. A keyed floor uses "<creator room name> floor" while the creator remains on that key; otherwise it uses the largest named room. Existing keys such as "own" without a creator use that fallback. A user-given plate name wins; the shared floor stays "Shared floor". Keyed rooms can have raised or sunken floor.elevation, stored as a level-local walking top. Slab thickness, foundation height and edge finish use set_room_floor_construction, updating every piece of the key. Update ceiling paint regions (ceiling.regions: [x, z] polygons with a finish, later wins), step finishes (floorStepFinish for every step of the room; floorStepOverrides: [{ key, step?, finish }] per doorway, key = the door id the step sits under or the lower room id), wall material and construction opt-outs. daylight { artificialLight, mechanicalVentilation } declares a habitable room lit and aired by artificial means (the IRC R303.1 exceptions to daylight; both true), stored in the room's metadata; a bedroom, living room or kitchen needs a window to outside or this declaration, above and below grade alike. Absent fields are unchanged; null clears.

anyOf.description: In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Minimum 0.02 m.
In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft").

artificialLight.description: The room is lit by artificial light.

mechanicalVentilation.description: The room is aired by mechanical ventilation.

tools.name: divide_zone
tools.title: Divide room
tools.description: Divide a room with an open path (endpoints snap to its boundary; the seed side keeps its id) or a closed island (outer room keeps its id). The two rooms are parted by a separator (the editor's Separator: a room boundary with no wall), not a wall. Supply path or the legacy two-point cut. Islands need 0.25 m² and 5 cm wall clearance.

tools.name: merge_zones
tools.title: Merge rooms
tools.description: Merge two rooms by removing the separators they share (the editor's Separator: a room boundary with no wall). Walls are preserved; wall-only boundaries return a conflict.

tools.name: delete_zone
tools.title: Delete room
tools.description: Delete a room. A room Divide made, which shares a separator (the editor's Separator: a room boundary with no wall) with a room on its outline, merges back into that room: the separators go, walls and items stay (mode "merge"). A room whose every boundary is a wall shared with other rooms is refused with a "shared-walls" conflict and nothing changes (mode "blocked"); delete one of its walls instead. Otherwise the room goes with its unshared walls, separators and their openings (mode "delete"), and contents chooses whether its items are kept or deleted. Returns the disposition payload.

tools.name: run_batch
tools.title: Run a batch of scene tools
tools.description: Optionally run several scene tools in one call: in order, each on the scene the calls before it left, applied as one undo step, with a report per call. Supports repeated or known-in-advance work; individual calls remain available. A call cannot use an id another call of the same batch creates; created ids are available in the report for subsequent calls. onRefusal stop (default): a refused call stops the batch and nothing is applied; skip: the others are applied and each refusal is reported; add_object calls are independent of each other under both: one that fails is reported with its own error and the others are applied, each with the receipt a single add_object gives. Tools: paint, search_materials, list_levels, get_node, get_level_summary, get_walls, get_zones, duplicate_level, verify_scene, delete_node, measure_stair, fit_stair, find_by_type, create_roof, add_wall, add_fence, add_level, create_stair, add_corner_window, merge_windows, add_column, add_object, place_design, place_in_room.

tool.description: One of the tools listed in the description.

input.description: That tool's input, as when calling it on its own.

onRefusal.description: stop (default): nothing is applied if a call is refused. skip: apply the rest.

tools.name: list_collections
tools.title: List collections
tools.description: List the scene's collections with their elements (id, name, type, level), and the templates a collection can start from.

tools.name: edit_collection
tools.title: Edit collection
tools.description: Create, rename, recolour or delete a collection, or add and remove its elements. A collection is a named set of any scene elements (lights, windows, doors, columns, objects built with add_object…), listed in the editor's Collections; being in one changes nothing about the elements. Without collectionId the call works on the scene's collection with that template, or else that name, and creates it when there is none.

template.description: Start from a template, which gives the name and colour unless you pass them.

name.description: Name of the collection, or its new name.

add.description: Ids of the elements to add.

remove.description: Ids of the elements to take out.

delete.description: Delete the collection; its elements stay in the scene.

tools.name: add_column
tools.title: Add column
tools.description: Add a structural or decorative column at (x, z), or rebuild one by nodeId. Supports native fields or optional code using the same module and conventions as add_object, with floor mount and its bottom centre at the support point. Params named height, width and depth drive the native size controls. Only add columns when requested.

x.description: X position of the column center (meters)

z.description: Z position of the column center (meters)

height.description: Column height (default: 2.5). In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Must be greater than 0 m.

radius.description: Radius when crossSection is "round" (default: 0.22). In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Must be greater than 0 m.

width.description: Width when crossSection is "square" / "rectangular" (default: 0.44). In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Must be greater than 0 m.

depth.description: Depth when crossSection is "square" / "rectangular" (default: 0.44). In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Must be greater than 0 m.

rotation.description: Y-axis rotation (default: 0). In degrees, or text with a unit ("1.57rad").

style.description: Visual style: 'plain' (default smooth pillar), 'faceted' (sharp prism faces), 'fluted' (vertical channels — classical), 'lathe-turned' (turned bands — porch / interior), 'dravidian-carved' (heavy carving — temple), 'cluster' (bundled colonnette — gothic).

level.description: Level id from list_levels; omitted uses the viewed or lowest level.

y.description: Support point height above the level, in metres (default 0).

name.description: What the user would call this design.

description.description: A short description of this design, at most 200 characters.

category.description: What this design is, in one or two words.

tags.description: Up to five short lowercase search tags, at most 32 characters each.

nodeId.description: Rebuild this column with code, params or native size fields; get_source provides current code when needed.

code.description: A module (three.js, or bpy with language) when the native fields cannot express the column. Same module and conventions as add_object; mount floor. Declare height, width and depth params for editable dimensions.

language.description: The code's language: 'three' (default) for a three.js module, 'bpy' for a Blender module (see add_object). On an edit it defaults to the language the object was built in.

params.description: Values for the params the module declares; on an edit, each one you leave out keeps its current value (clamped to the param's range) and a param new to the code starts at its default.

tools.name: add_object
tools.title: Build object
tools.description:
Author parametric Three.js furniture, decor and custom objects of any shape, dimensions or style, whether or not the catalog holds something similar (the catalog is a limited set that varies by server). Examples include a low oak table, a slatted bench, a paper lantern, built-ins, custom columns and capitals, mouldings and trim, panels, exposed beams, ceiling bodies, canopies, a porch and railings. Pascal runs the module in a sandbox, stores the result and places it as one object the user can move, paint, and ask you to edit again.

Module shape (import THREE from the three package as usual; the addons below too):
  // also available: three/addons/utils/BufferGeometryUtils.js, three/addons/geometries/{RoundedBoxGeometry,ConvexGeometry,LoftGeometry,ParametricGeometry}.js, three-bvh-csg (Brush, Evaluator, SUBTRACTION, ADDITION, INTERSECTION)
  export const params = { width: { default: 4.8, min: 3, max: 8, step: 0.1, unit: 'm', label: 'Width' } }
  export const mount = 'floor'   // 'floor' | 'wall-side' (on a wall face) | 'wall' (through a wall, like a window) | 'ceiling'
  export default function build({ params, THREE }) { const group = new THREE.Group(); /* … */ return group }

One object is one feature that changes together: a table, a bench, a porch, a railing run, a fireplace surround, a ceiling with its beams. Never a whole house, and never walls, rooms, floors, roofs, stairs, doors or windows: those have their own tools. A new object's reason records its design intent: what the authored shape, dimensions or style contributes to the request. The scene check lists every authored object with its reason; no catalog-exhaustion proof is required. On a floor, a plain box with a wall's size or a floor plate is refused with the tool to use (use_walls, use_slab); a detailed object with a wall's size (a bookcase, a screen), or one named after something Pascal builds, is built with a hint naming the tool.

Conventions (they make the object work in Pascal; follow them):
- Metres, Y up, modelled in its installed orientation. Floor and wall mounts put the bottom-centre of the visible bounds at the placement point. Ceiling mounts put the top-centre there: visible geometry extends down in negative local Y, with its top at Y = 0. Wall-side mounts put the bottom-centre of the back face there (back at Z = 0, facing +Z). Normalization translates geometry; it does not flip it.
- Paint: name every material slot_<finish> (slot_trim, slot_frame, slot_metal) and reuse one material per finish; a material named "glass" renders as glass.
- Parts: name the few groups a person would point at part:<id> (part:column_left, part:canopy, part:landing), usually 2–24, a group per part, not every mesh. Set userData.type on parts someone would look for: column, beam, slab, roof, railing, panel, trim, step, light.
- Lights: add a THREE.PointLight or SpotLight named light:<id> where the bulb is; it becomes a switchable light.
- Motion: put THREE.AnimationClips on the returned group's .animations, as in any three.js project; tracks target <objectName>.<property> or <object.uuid>.<property> and may use any transform property (position, rotation, rotation[y], quaternion, scale); material and visibility tracks do not animate. A clip named open becomes the object's open/close control (close plays a clip named close, or open reversed); a clip named loop runs continuously; every other clip gets its own play toggle labelled with its name (name it for the person: "Twirl", "Music"). Write as many clips as the object needs.
- Cuts: a mesh named cutout cuts only the mounted host; cut:wall, cut:ceiling and cut:slab require that host kind (floor items cut their support slab). The hidden cutter must reach the host; walls use its real shape, ceilings and slabs its through-hole footprint.
- Sockets: an empty Object3D named anchor:<id> marks where other things attach.
- No textures, network or DOM. At most 300k triangles, 32 materials, 60 m per side.

Blender instead (language 'bpy'): when the shape is easier with Blender's modelling (bevelled or rounded edges, subdivision-smooth and organic forms, booleans, curves and text, solidify, array, screw and other modifiers), write a bpy module:
  import bpy, bmesh
  PARAMS = {"width": {"default": 1.8, "min": 1.2, "max": 2.6, "step": 0.05, "unit": "m", "label": "Width"}}
  MOUNT = "floor"
  def build(params): ...   # add objects to the empty scene; everything in it is exported, modifiers applied
The same conventions in Blender terms: metres, Z up, the front faces -Y (Blender's Front view); part:<id>, light:<id> (a light object; its custom property intensity sets the brightness, default 2), anchor:<id> (an empty), cutout, cut:wall|ceiling|slab and collider are object names; userData is the object's custom properties (obj["type"] = "panel"); slot_<finish> are material names. A clip is one action named open, close, loop or anything else, assigned to every object that moves in it. Use the data API and bmesh, not operators that need a 3D viewport. A Blender build takes a few seconds.

Several objects: they do not depend on each other, so several add_object calls can go in one step, or in one run_batch call (a call per object; each is reported on its own with its receipt, and one that fails does not stop the others).

Edit: pass nodeId with new code and/or params (params alone rebuild the stored script; get_source provides the current code and params when needed); identity, placement, paint and the params you leave out are kept. The result lists the size, parts, slots, lights, animations and params.

code.description: The module (see the tool description). Required to create; omit to rebuild an object with new params.

language.description: The code's language: 'three' (default) for a three.js module, 'bpy' for a Blender module (see add_object). On an edit it defaults to the language the object was built in.

params.description: Values for the params the module declares; on an edit, each one you leave out keeps its current value (clamped to the param's range) and a param new to the code starts at its default.

nodeId.description: Edit this existing authored object instead of creating one.

parentId.description: Host for a new object: a level (default: the floor in view), a wall (wall / wall-side mounts), a ceiling, or an item it rests on.

position.description: Placement of the mount origin in the host frame, metres. Floor: [x, y, z] locates the bottom-centre (y = 0 on the level floor). Ceiling: [x, y, z] locates the top-centre (y = 0 on the drawn ceiling attachment plane; negative y lowers it). Wall / wall-side: [distance along the wall from its start, height of the bottom, 0]; wall-side also anchors the back face.

rotation.description: Y-axis rotation in the host frame. New wall-side back mounts default to 180° so +Z faces away from the wall; other new objects default to 0°. An edit keeps its saved rotation unless given. In degrees, or text with a unit ("1.57rad").

side.description: Which wall face a wall-side object sits on.

name.description: What the user would call it ("Low oak table").

description.description: A short description of this design, at most 200 characters.

category.description: What it is, one word or two ("table", "bench", "porch", "lantern", "trim").

tags.description: Up to five short lowercase search tags, at most 32 characters each.

reason.description: Design intent: why this authored shape, size or style suits the request ("low oak table for the Japandi seating area"). Required to create; an edit keeps it unless given. No catalog-exhaustion proof is required.

tools.name: author_scene
tools.title: Author scene
tools.description:
Turn a whole design you wrote as free three.js into an editable Pascal scene, in one call. You read your own module however you like (its source, running it and reading the objects, both) and hand over a conversion payload: levels, walls with their openings, rooms, slabs, columns, railings, every piece of furniture as an authored object with its own module, and lights. Pascal does the rest server-side: compiles and stores each item, places it, derives the rooms and their floors, paints, runs its checks, saves, and answers with a gate report you iterate against. Nothing you hand over is silently dropped: what cannot be placed comes back by name with a reason, and what Pascal corrected (a wall end snapped onto the centerline it meets) is listed.

Coordinates: metres, plan x/z, Y up, each level's floor at y = 0 in its own frame. A wall is its centerline; walls meet where centerlines meet, so end a partition on the centerline of the wall it runs into. An opening's 'along' is measured from the wall's start to the opening's centre; give each opening its type (how it opens) and style (its look), or its own module for a shape they cannot express. An item's position is where its bottom centre stands; its module follows the add_object contract (metres, Y up, built in its installed orientation; at most 300k triangles and 32 materials per item; name materials slot_<finish>; drawers, doors and lids as animation clips; a THREE light named light:<id> where a bulb is). A hex colour is written as an exact material, one per distinct colour. Pascal builds a wall's cap, the floor plate and the ceiling itself: fold a module's caps, underlays and floor planks into the wall, the room's floor finish and the room (say so in notes), never into slabs or regions: baseboards are the wall's skirting, a plank or tile floor is the room's floorCode, tiles, panelling or boards on a wall are its faceLeft / faceRight (or the room's wallCode); a slab is a terrace, a platform, a balcony. Build the building as it is built: a wall at its real height, nothing lowered or removed for viewing.

The report says what was written, what Pascal defaulted (defaults: a window with no type is fixed and cannot open), what it warns about but wrote (warnings: thin slabs, too many slabs or regions) and what it refused (defects, by your ids).

Call again with the same scene and a corrected payload to update the previous conversion (replace: true). Stable element identities and manual changes are retained; overlapping changes are refused. An existing building without a conversion baseline is never cleared.

elevation.description: The level's floor height above the ground floor's (default 0). In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Default 0 m.

id.description: Your own id, unique across every wall and item on all levels.

height.description: Wall height. In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Must be greater than 0 m.

thickness.description: Wall thickness. In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Must be greater than 0 m.

color.description: Paint for both faces: #rrggbb, written as an exact material, or a library ref (library:<id>) from search_materials.

colorLeft.description: Paint for the face on the left when looking from start to end, same forms as color; over color. The left is the wall's front.

colorRight.description: Paint for the face on the right when looking from start to end, same forms as color; over color.

along.description: From the wall's start to the opening's centre, along the centerline. In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft").

width.description: Opening width. In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Must be greater than 0 m.

height.description: Opening height. In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Must be greater than 0 m.

sill.description: Bottom of the opening above the floor; 0 for a door or floor-to-ceiling glazing (default 0). In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Default 0 m.

Over the room's wallCode. The report warns when the build leaves part of the face uncovered.

code.description: The face's finish: a three.js module that builds this face's finish (tiles with joints, panelling, boards) for exactly the face: it receives params.outline, params.holes (its doors and windows), params.base and params.thickness in wall-local metres (x along the wall from its start, y up from the face's base, z out of the face) and lays the finish out: Pascal cuts the build to the outline and its openings, so tiles and boards may run past the edges and over the doors and windows (the holes are there for a layout that wants them, tiles centred on a window); Pascal rebuilds it when the wall or its openings change.

tools.name: get_source
tools.title: Read object script
tools.description: The module (three.js or Blender bpy, named by language) an object (or a window, door or column built from code) runs, with its params and their current values; a room's id reads its floor script, the module that builds its floor finish; a wall's id with face reads that face's script (face may be left out when only one face has one). Optional source evidence when the current module is needed. An edited module can be passed back with the same nodeId: to add_object for an object, to add_window / add_door / add_column for their respective kinds.

nodeId.description: An object, window, door or column built from code, a room with a floor script, or a wall with a face script.

face.description: A wall's face whose script to read; needed when both faces have one.

tools.name: measure
tools.title: Measure
tools.description: Measure the distance (in meters) between two nodes, or the net area of a polygon node when fromId === toId. Distance is between world-space reference points, returned as fromPoint/toPoint: a positioned node's origin in its host's frame (an item's base, a door's or window's centre in its wall), a wall's or fence's midpoint at its base, a slab's, ceiling's or zone's polygon centroid on its plane, a block's or imported mesh's vertex-bounds centre, a level's plan centre on its base plane, and another container's descendants' centre. `approximate` lists nodes whose renderer derives the pose from data not modelled here (a downspout at its gutter outlet, a gutter at the eave), with the reason.

tools.name: view_scene
tools.title: Look at the scene
tools.description: Look at the building in 3D from a viewpoint you pick and get the picture back: the finished house, every storey and the roof by default, or an explicit Solo/Exploded level presentation, whatever view mode the person has on. Use it to compare what you built with a reference and say what differs before you fix it: the facade from the photo's own camera (camera: its position, aim, field of view and aspect), rendered at the photo's aspect to lay beside it; or from the photo's side at street height (from 'street', 'street-left', …, eyeHeight 1.7), in its light (lighting); one face square on (projection orthographic); the massing from above, or an aerial view (elevation 40). The view frames the target (a building, a level, a wall or a zone; the whole building, its roof included, by default) from outside, unless you place the eye yourself with position or camera. To stand inside a room and see its furniture and finishes at a person's height, give interior {zoneId} (a room: an id from get_zones or create_room): the eye stands in the room a step in from a corner, looking across it, with the cut below; from picks the side of the room it stands on, target something in the room to look at it. To see inside a floor, give interior {levelId}: the other floors and that floor's roofs and ceilings are left out of the picture, and everything on it, walls, openings and furniture alike, is cut at 0.65 of the storey's height (about two thirds), so a tall wardrobe or a door head is cut, not short; a roof level has no inside; with no eye given it looks down into the floor, or into the room or zone you target. A level below grade, targeted alone, is looked into the same way (from outside the ground would cover it), the ground over it drawn as a faint veil. The live view is not changed. A door, a window or an item on a floor frames at detail scale, an opening seen from its outside face: a close-up to lay beside the photo's crop of the same element, to see what differs. Over the MCP the user's editor tab open on the project renders the picture: with none open it is refused (editor_tab_required), a tab in the background must be brought to the front (editor_tab_hidden), and a tab that is open but busy or still loading answers editor_tab_busy: call view_scene again in a few seconds, the user need not be asked. Where the host keeps the picture it answers its viewId: name it to use that exact frame later (a Studio render of this view) without taking it again. A picture is not a measure: take sizes and counts from the tools.

target.description: A building, level, wall, zone, door, window or floor item id to frame. Default: every storey in the scene, walls and roofs.

interior.description: Look inside, with one of: levelId (a floor): the other floors and its roofs and ceilings are left out of the picture, everything on it (walls, openings, furniture) cut at 0.65 of the storey height. Default framing looks down into it; camera or position still wins. zoneId (a room: an id from get_zones or create_room): the same cut, and the eye stands inside the room at a person's height (1.6 m, or eyeHeight), a step in from its corner farthest from what it looks at (from picks the corner on that side), looking across the room with a 75 degree field of view (fov changes it); with a target on the floor it looks at the target. position, elevation, from above or projection orthographic put the eye outside again, over the cut room.

presentation.description: Verify the actual level presentation: stacked (default), exploded, or solo with a levelId. Solo keeps full-height geometry, including ceilings and any roofs incorrectly owned by that floor; it is not the clipped interior view. Does not change the live view. Do not combine with interior.

from.description: The side the eye stands on: a compass side (north is the plan's top edge, z grows south, x east), above, or a side as a front photo names it, standing in the street facing the house ('street-left' is its left front corner, 'back' the far side), from the street the site records, else the house's own front (its -z, the way a generated house faces). Default south-west.

elevation.description: Degrees above the horizon the eye looks down from: 35 to 60 for an aerial view. Default 12. In degrees, or text with a unit ("1.57rad"). Range -10–89 deg.

eyeHeight.description: Metres above the ground for a street view (1.7), instead of elevation. In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Minimum 0 m.

position.description: The eye exactly, [x, height, z] in metres; it looks at the target.

fov.description: Vertical field of view in degrees for a perspective view. Default 45. In degrees, or text with a unit ("1.57rad"). Range 10–100 deg.

projection.description: orthographic for a square-on elevation of a face, no perspective.

camera.description: A photo's camera (position, target, fov, aspect): the render takes its eye, aim and field of view at the photo's aspect. Or 'current': the person's own view, as their editor shows it now (the MCP has none: no_current_camera). Not with from, position, elevation, eyeHeight, fov or projection.

lighting.description: The light the picture is rendered in: the scene's own (current, the default), or day, overcast, sunset, dusk (twilight, the lights on) or night, as a reference photo was taken in.

maxPx.description: The picture's longest side in pixels, for a smaller one. Default 1920 by 1200, and never longer than 1920.

photo.description: The photo's crop of the element the view frames, returned beside it in the same call: a door's glass, a lamp's shape, a window's panes, at detail scale, to say what differs.

source.description: The photo as a data:image/...;base64 URL (read the file and encode it); in the chat, the URL of a file the user attached works too.

region.description: [left, top, right, bottom] in the photo's pixels: the element to compare.

tools.name: apply_patch
tools.title: Apply patch
tools.description: Apply a batch of create/update/delete operations atomically. All patches are validated before any are applied; the entire batch forms a single undo step. Batch-first is the default: prefer one apply_patch call containing all create/update/delete ops for a build step, in stable order so later ops can reference ids created by earlier ops. A single call is atomic (all or nothing) and pays the snapshot and save cost once; do not loop one-op calls. A create whose id already exists fails the whole patch with node_exists; to replace a node, delete it earlier in the same patch. An update cannot change id or type (identity_change) or object or children (immutable_field); restating the current value is fine. A parentId change must name an existing node that holds children (invalid_parent). An update cannot add schema issues to a node (invalid_update). After a delete or a roof update that regenerates a roof's default gutters, those gutters and their downspouts are addressable only in a later call (regenerated_default). A roof created or moved onto the storey whose walls carry it goes to the level above them (the roof level over a top storey), said in notes; storey content (walls, zones, slabs, ceilings, items, stairs) on a roof level (roof_level), a walled level declared the roof level (roof_level_holds_storey) and floor indexes putting a roof level under a storey (roof_level_on_top) are refused. Refusals come back as a tool error whose text is JSON {code, patchIndex, id, message}.

name.description: Optional display name for the saved scene. Defaults to the template name.

tools.name: create_house_from_brief
tools.title: Create house from brief
tools.description: High-level hosted workflow for external agents: choose a starter house from a brief, create/save/publish it, and return the editor URL. Use semantic tools afterward for exact customization.

tools.name: create_project
tools.title: Create project
tools.description: Create a browser-visible Pascal project for the authenticated user. Use this before save_scene when the user asks for a new project.

tools.name: get_project_status
tools.title: Get project status
tools.description: Authoritative status/debug call for a Pascal project: editor URL, browser-visible version, latest saved version, published version, node count, and graph hash.

tools.name: save_scene
tools.title: Save scene
tools.description: Save the current scene (or a provided graph) to the SceneStore. Without id or projectId it saves to the project this session is bound to (create_project or load_scene). Defaults to a browser-visible draft save so agents can iterate without creating many project versions. Use saveMode: "checkpoint" for meaningful version history.

replace.description: Write this session's scene over a project or scene it was not loaded from, replacing what that one holds.

saveMode.description: `draft` updates the browser-visible working model without polluting version history. `checkpoint` creates a meaningful saved version; it does not publish.

publish.description: Hosted Pascal: also publish this checkpoint, making it the version the project's viewers see. Only when the user asks to publish.

includeCurrentScene.description: If true, save the bridge current scene. If false, use the graph arg.

graph.description: Full SceneGraph { nodes, rootNodeIds, collections? } to save instead of the bridge state. Judged against the scene it is saved over (the session's scene when the save goes to it, else the stored scene `id` names) as apply_patch is: a roof it puts on the walls of the storey holding it goes to the level above them, said in notes, and storey content on a roof level is refused. A graph with no scene under it is saved as it is.

tools.name: load_scene
tools.title: Load scene
tools.description: Load a scene from the SceneStore into the bridge. Returns the scene metadata. Throws `scene_not_found` if the id does not exist.

tools.name: list_scenes
tools.title: List scenes
tools.description: List scenes in the SceneStore. Optionally filter by `projectId` and cap results with `limit` (default 100).

tools.name: delete_scene
tools.title: Delete scene
tools.description: Remove a stored scene by id. In Pascal this never deletes the project: it hides it from Pascal's public listings until it is next saved with content, and answers `deleted: false, hidden: true` with a message; its owner can delete it from the projects page. Only someone who can manage the project may hide it. A local scene store deletes the scene. Optionally pass `expectedVersion` for optimistic concurrency.

tools.name: rename_scene
tools.title: Rename scene
tools.description: Rename a scene in the SceneStore. Returns the updated SceneMeta. Optionally pass `expectedVersion` for optimistic concurrency.

tools.name: generate_variants
tools.title: Generate variants
tools.description: Generate N variations of a base scene by forking and applying seeded mutations. Example: "give me 5 variations of this kitchen". If `save=true`, each variant is persisted via scene operations and returned with an id + URL; otherwise the graph is returned inline.

baseSceneId.description: If set, fork from this saved scene; else fork from current bridge state.

save.description: If true, also save each variant via SceneStore and return ids.

tools.name: photo_to_scene
tools.title: Photo to Pascal scene
tools.description: Orchestrator: analyse a floor-plan photo via MCP sampling, translate the structured vision result into a Pascal SceneGraph (site → building → level with walls and zones), optionally save it, and swap the bridge to the new scene. Requires host support for sampling.

image.description: Base64 or https URL of the floor-plan photo

defaultWallThickness.description: Default wall thickness. In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Must be greater than 0 m.

defaultWallHeight.description: Default wall height. In metres, or text with a unit ("6 ft"). Must be greater than 0 m.

tools.name: analyze_floorplan_image
tools.title: Analyze floor-plan image
tools.description: Defer to the MCP host (via sampling) to extract walls, rooms, and approximate dimensions from a floor-plan image. Requires host support for sampling.

scaleHint.description: Text hint about scale, e.g. '1 cm = 1 m' or 'approximately 80 m²'

tools.name: analyze_room_photo
tools.title: Analyze room photo
tools.description: Defer to the MCP host (via sampling) to extract approximate dimensions, fixtures, and windows from a single-room photograph. Requires host support for sampling.
